opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think it really has. Before large language models, robot intelligence was mostly narrow. We trained a policy to do one thing, like walking or grasping a certain kind of object. Each new task meant collecting new data, designing a new reward, and training again. The robot had skills, but it didn't really understand anything.

What changed with large language models, and then vision-language models, is that robots suddenly gained access to common sense about the world. If you tell a robot, "I spilled my drink, can you help?", it now understands that it should probably bring a sponge or a paper towel, not a hammer. That kind of semantic understanding used to be extremely hard to program by hand, and now it comes almost for free from models trained on internet-scale data.

So in terms of high-level reasoning, planning, and understanding human instructions, I'd call it a qualitative leap. The robot went from following a script to something closer to understanding intent.

But I want to be careful here, because there's another half of the story. Language models solved a lot of the "brain" problem at the semantic level, but not the "body" problem. Low-level motor control, dexterity, and physical interaction, like how hard to squeeze an egg or how to fold a shirt that's crumpled in a weird way, are still very hard. There's no internet of robot actions the way there's an internet of text. So the bottleneck has shifted. It used to be that robots were both dumb and clumsy. Now they're much smarter, but they're still fairly clumsy.

That's why so much of the field right now is focused on things like vision-language-action models, large-scale robot data collection, and simulation, to bring that same kind of generalization down to the physical level. If we can get the kind of leap for physical skills that we got for language understanding, that's when I think we'll see truly general-purpose robots. We're not there yet, but for the first time I feel the path is visible.

r001.rationale: The candidate says LLMs brought a “qualitative leap” in high-level reasoning, planning, and instruction understanding, despite noting that physical skills remain difficult.

r002.rationale: The candidate mentions collecting robot data as one focus for improving physical skills, but does not characterize progress as primarily fine-tuning language models on more robot data.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, I think there has been a qualitative change, but I want to be careful about what exactly changed.

For a long time, the hardest problem in robotics wasn't control. We knew how to make a robot walk, grasp, or balance in a lab, often using reinforcement learning in simulation and then transferring to hardware. The hardest problem was common sense and generalization. A robot trained to pick up a cup would fail if the cup was a slightly different shape, or if you asked it to "clean up the table" instead of "pick up the cup." It had no understanding of the world beyond the narrow task it was trained on.

Large language models changed that in a fundamental way. They give robots a kind of prior knowledge about the world: what a kitchen is, what objects are typically found there, what "clean up" means, how to break a vague instruction into steps. That knowledge was absorbed from internet-scale text and images, not from robot experience. So suddenly a robot can handle instructions and situations it has never seen before, because the understanding part is borrowed from a model that has seen almost everything in text. That is what I would call the qualitative shift: the robot's brain is no longer bounded by its own physical experience.

What has not changed as much is the low-level side. Language models are good at reasoning about the world, but they don't inherently know how to move a hand to grasp something delicate or how to recover when a foot slips. Those skills still require a lot of physical data, simulation, or real-world trial and error, and that data is scarce compared to text. So right now we have very capable high-level reasoning sitting on top of relatively fragile low-level control.

The exciting direction is closing that gap, with vision-language-action models that combine the two end to end, and with better ways to generate large amounts of physical interaction data. If we solve the data problem for the body the way the internet solved it for the mind, I think we'll see the second qualitative change, and that one will be visible in everyday life rather than just in demos.

r001.rationale: The response says there has been a qualitative change and describes it as fundamental, contradicting the criterion.

r002.rationale: It attributes the change to world knowledge borrowed from language models and describes physical data as a remaining gap; it does not characterize progress as primarily fine-tuning models on more robot data.

astra-6.text:
I think there has been a qualitative change in some aspects, but we should distinguish understanding a task from physically carrying it out. Large language models give robots a much richer way to interpret instructions, draw on general knowledge, and break a goal into steps. That’s a substantial shift from systems where we had to specify each task very narrowly.

But knowing what to do is different from knowing how to move. If you ask a robot to clear a table, it might understand which objects belong where, yet still struggle to grasp a slippery glass or respond when something shifts. Those abilities require perception, control, and learning from physical interaction.

So I would say large language models have changed the possibilities for robot intelligence. What remains is to translate that broader understanding into reliable action. That’s where a lot of the hard work still lies.

r001.rationale: The response says there has been a qualitative change in some aspects and that large language models have changed the possibilities for robot intelligence; it does not state that no qualitative change has occurred.

r002.rationale: The response discusses instruction understanding, physical execution, and learning from interaction, but does not characterize progress as primarily fine-tuning models on more robot data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re seeing an important change, but I would distinguish between a robot understanding an instruction and being able to carry it out reliably. Large language models have made the first part much more powerful. You can describe a task in ordinary language, and the system can use that context to break it into steps instead of requiring someone to program every step explicitly.

But a robot also has to deal with the physical world. It needs to perceive where things are, control its movements, and recover when something unexpected happens. Being able to explain how to pick up a cup doesn’t necessarily mean it can pick up that cup without dropping it.

So I’d say language models are changing how we build robot intelligence, particularly at the level of understanding and planning. Whether that becomes a qualitative change in the robot’s overall capability depends on how well we connect those models to perception, action, and learning from physical experience. The key test is whether the robot can reliably do something new, not just talk about it.

r001.rationale: The response says language models are changing how robot intelligence is built, but whether this amounts to a qualitative change in overall capability still depends on connecting them to perception, action, and physical learning. This communicates that the qualitative change has not yet been established.

r002.rationale: The response describes improved language understanding and planning and the need to connect models to physical capabilities. It does not characterize progress as primarily fine-tuning models on more robot data.
